name: baritone-behind-the-beat
idea: A deep, calm male baritone with a little gravel, rapping slightly behind the beat like a man who never needs to hurry, every syllable clear and each rule ending with space before the next. Ask for the music the way a producer would, as a short list of parts: late-1990s East Coast boom bap at about 86 BPM, a dusty sampled drum break with a hard snare on 2 and 4, a looped upright bass phrase, a muted jazz piano chop, and light vinyl crackle, warm and slightly lo-fi. In the lyrics, tag each rule as its own small section with a direction like [two-bar drum break, then] before it, so every "Number ..." lands on the downbeat after a clear gap. Put trap hi-hats, auto-tune, sung hooks and fast double-time in Exclude, and keep Variety low so the loop stays steady.

name: street-tenor-horn-stabs
idea: A higher, nasal, slightly raspy young male tenor with a confident street-corner bark, punchy and rhythmic but never rushed: he states each number on its own, takes a breath, then delivers the line. Ask for the music as a scene and mood rather than an instrument list: a cold late-night New York block in 1997, tense and sly, built on a short brooding horn-and-strings sample that stabs once on every number, a heavy kick, and a cracking snare at around 90 BPM. Between rules, ask for a short instrumental turntable cut or record-scratch fill (no words) so the countdown feels like it is being counted off by the DJ. Use lyric directions like [punchy, deliberate, one bar per line] and keep the closing fix line alone over a stripped drop to just the drums.

name: weathered-ledger-reader
idea: An older, weathered male voice, low and raspy, half-spoken and half-rapped, conversational and dry, like a veteran reading house rules out of a worn ledger to a new recruit; the intro "Uh. Money printer manual. Take notes." is marked [Spoken] over almost nothing. Ask for the music as a minimal arrangement in plain words: slow head-nod boom bap at about 82 BPM, just kick, rimshot snare, a soft repeating Rhodes chord and a low bass note, very sparse with lots of air, so the voice sits right on top. Structure the lyric as ten very short verses with a [Slow Flow] direction at the top and a [Break] line before each rule, and let the music thin to near silence before the final fix line, which he says plainly. Keep the mood wry and patient, not aggressive, and put choir, sung chorus, trap drums and auto-tune in Exclude.
